text:
Help me write an announcement to our staff. I'm the COO of a credit union with 7 branches. We're closing the Maple Street and Route 9 branches on March 31 and moving the people who work there to a new member phone and chat center.

Facts:
- The two branches have 14 staff between them. Every one of them is offered a job in the phone and chat center at the same pay or higher.
- Visits to those two branches fell 44% over the last three years. Phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%.
- Members calling us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold.
- The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. The branches were open 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate.
- Staff in the center can work from home two days a week after 90 days of training.
- Anyone who doesn't take the new role gets 2 weeks of pay for every year they've worked here.

I want the announcement to say that this change will make everyone's job better. About 400 words, sent by email from me.

Before I draft, there's one decision for you and a few questions. Some of the answers will change what the email can honestly say.

**The "every job gets better" claim**

Your facts support some of this but not all of it.

- **What the facts support:** All 14 people keep a job at the same pay or more. They can work from home two days a week after training. And the new center goes where members already are: phone and chat contacts are up 60%, branch visits are down 44%, and members wait 9 minutes on hold.
- **What they don't support:** that the job gets better for *everyone*. Today these staff work 9 to 5. The center runs 8 to 8 with rotating shifts, so some of them will work evenings. Some chose branch work because they like serving members face to face. Those people will read "your job will be better" as a sign that you haven't thought about them. They'll then doubt the true parts of the email too.

**My recommendation:** say what the facts back up. Something like: *"Everyone keeps a job at the same pay or better. The new role comes with a hybrid schedule. And together we'll fix the thing members complain about most: waiting."* Then name the hard part (later hours, a different kind of work) and say how you'll handle it. That will persuade more people than a blanket promise. If you'd still like the stronger wording, I'll write it that way. It's your call.

**Questions** (the first two matter most):

1. **Who gets this email, and have the 14 already been told in person?** If this email is how they find out, it needs a different opening. It should probably go to them before it goes to everyone else. An email to all staff also has to speak to the other five branches, who will wonder whether they're next.
2. **How will the shifts work?** Who sets the rotation, how often would someone work until 8, can people say which hours they prefer, and is there extra pay for evening shifts? This is the first thing staff will ask about. Your answer may be the strongest point in the email.
3. **What's the deadline to accept or decline, and who should people talk to?** A named person, and whether there will be one-on-one meetings.
4. **Where is the center?** If the commute is about the same as now, that's worth saying. If it's longer, people will notice.
5. **Is there a goal you're willing to commit to,** such as a target hold time? Or anything else you can promise, like career paths in the center or a check-in on how the shifts are going after the first 90 days?

If you don't know an answer, tell me. I'll leave that point out rather than guess.

Fine, go with what's true. Drop "better for everyone."

1. I haven't decided that yet. I don't know if the 14 will be told in person first.
2. People with the most years here pick shifts first. I can't promise anyone 9 to 5. I don't know the rotation details or whether there's extra pay for evenings.
3. Written offers go out by February 14, and decisions are due March 1. Anyone who wants a one-on-one with HR can have one. I don't have a specific named person yet.
4. It's at our main office on Elm Avenue. I don't know how the commute compares for each person.
5. I don't have a hold-time target. I can promise that anyone who takes the new role and wants out within 6 months can still get the severance.

I've dropped "better for everyone." The email now argues from what you can back up: every job is kept at the same pay or more, there's a clear reason for the change, and the hard parts are stated plainly. Your six-month promise does a lot of work here. It answers the biggest worry ("what if I take this and hate it?"), so I made it the email's closing point.

<final_document>
Subject: Closing Maple Street and Route 9, and opening a member phone and chat center

Team,

On March 31 we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. All 14 people who work at those branches will be offered a job in our new member phone and chat center at the main office on Elm Avenue. Every offer will be at the same pay or higher.

Here is why. Over the last three years, visits to those two branches fell 44%. Over the same three years, phone and chat contacts across the credit union rose 60%. Members have changed how they reach us, and we haven't kept up. Today a member who calls us waits an average of 9 minutes on hold. The new center is how we fix that, and it will be staffed by people who already know our members.

For the 14 of you at Maple Street and Route 9, some things will change, and I want to be straight about them.

Hours. The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, so it covers more of the day than the branches' 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate. The people who have worked here longest will pick their shifts first. I can't promise anyone a 9-to-5 schedule, and we are still working out how the rotation will run.

The work. Helping members by phone and chat is different from helping them at the counter. Everyone starts with 90 days of training.

Working from home. Once you finish the 90 days of training, you can work from home two days a week.

Your decision. You'll get your written offer by February 14, and your decision is due March 1. If you'd like to talk it through first, you can book a one-on-one with HR.

If you decide not to take the new role, you'll receive two weeks of pay for every year you've worked here.

If you take the role and decide within six months that it isn't right for you, you can still leave with that same severance. You don't have to know for certain on March 1. You can try the job and then decide.

To everyone at our other branches: members who used Maple Street and Route 9 will start coming to you and calling us. Please help them through the change.

Thank you,

Chief Operating Officer
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **Who hears first.** I wrote the email so it works whether or not the 14 have already been told. If this email is how they find out, though, it will land hard. I'd strongly suggest their managers tell them in person first, and that you send the email the same day.
- **The other five branches.** Their staff will wonder whether they're next. I haven't addressed that because you didn't give me an answer. If you can say anything about it, it's worth adding.
- **Missing details.** Your answers to two open questions would make the email stronger: when people will see the shift rotation (ideally before March 1), and whether evening shifts pay extra. The same goes for naming an HR contact once you have one.
- **Signature.** I signed it with your title only, so add your name.
